about: Narration for three Shorts cut from the hauntings documentary (Oct. 21, 2026; Scoop: "do all of these"). Every fact is from the documentary and its sources: the 1905 headless-ghost stories (The Virginia Enterprise, July 7, 1905, for Frank and George Place, the three shrieks and the river; the Muncie Evening Press, July 31, 1905, and the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier, Aug. 14, 1905, for the water tank, the dinner pail and Columbus Cole run over by an engine; the Barbour County Index, Aug. 16, 1905, for the boiler explosion); Charles Cathcart's own account of the Poston circle and his "lightning bug", in Emma Hardinge's Modern American Spiritualism (1870); Harriet Colfax from the National Park Service, Hoosier State Chronicles, her log (May 28, 1873) and the Chicago Daily Tribune, Oct. 2, 1904. Pushing a change here on the haunts-doc branch records it again (.github/workflows/haunts-shorts-voice.yml).

lines.say: In 1905, newspapers said a headless ghost was flagging trains near La Porte, Indiana.
lines.tts: In nineteen oh five, newspapers said a headless ghost was flagging trains near La Porte, Indiana.

lines.say: It stood by an old water tank, swinging its arms, a dinner pail in its hand.
Two men, Frank and George Place, said it gave three unearthly shrieks and disappeared toward the river.
People said it was Columbus Cole, who'd died years before. But the papers couldn't even agree on how.
The full story is in our documentary, Haunted La Porte County.
In the 1850s, a former congressman from La Porte set out to catch the spirits in the act.
lines.tts: In the eighteen fifties, a former congressman from La Porte set out to catch the spirits in the act.

lines.say: Charles Cathcart built a little paper tube of chemicals that would light up a dark room in a flash. He called it his lightning bug.
The lights went out. A drum began to play. He slipped his lightning bug onto the table.
In the light, he wrote, the drumstick was beating the drum, with no one within about eight feet of it.
The skeptic became a believer. The full story is in our documentary, Haunted La Porte County.
For forty-three years, a woman climbed to the same lamp in Michigan City, Indiana, every night, and lit it.
Harriet Colfax rowed across the creek to tend the pier light. Once, her log says, she was nearly swept into the lake.
In 1904, at about eighty, she retired. A Chicago paper quoted her: I could not bear to see anyone else light my lamp.
lines.tts: In nineteen oh four, at about eighty, she retired. A Chicago paper quoted her: I could not bear to see anyone else light my lamp.

lines.say: Six days later, the old lighthouse went dark for good. Some people say she's still keeping watch.
The full story is in our documentary, Haunted La Porte County.
